title: Kirby's Dream Land
principle: Earn replay value through fun, not unreasonable difficulty
why: Limited NES cartridge memory pushed games to be tough so players wouldn't finish too quickly, but unreasonable difficulty shut out beginners; like arcade games, a fun game gets played again and again.
how: Aim for play that feels good to repeat rather than padding a short game with punishing difficulty.
anti_pattern: Using difficulty as a substitute for content.
example: NES-era hard games vs. Kirby's Dream Land.
quote: If it's fun, you'll play it again and again.

title: Kirby Super Star
principle: Check a new production technique fits before adopting it mid-project
why: Kirby Super Star switched to CG backgrounds mid-development following the Donkey Kong Country trend; the staff weren't familiar with it and it didn't fit Kirby's pieced-together terrain, though learning new skills still matters.
how: Before adopting a trendy technique, confirm the team knows it and it suits how levels are built; treat it as skill-building if you proceed.
anti_pattern: Following an art trend that doesn't fit your game.
quote: Still, it's important to learn new skills. The things you make today can lead to what you make tomorrow.

title: Super Smash Bros.
principle: Design your concept to solve a specific problem in its genre.
why: He felt combo-focused fighters lost push and pull: after the first hit the opponent's skill was irrelevant and newcomers just watched themselves lose.
how: List the genre's pain points, then design a core rule that removes them, as accumulated damage and ring-outs created room for interplay and improvisation.
anti_pattern: Letting inputs alone decide the outcome after the first hit.
example: Super Smash Bros.' accumulated damage system.
quote: Instead of inputs alone determining the outcome, I wondered if we could make a game with more room for interplay and improvisation.

title: Super Smash Bros. Melee
principle: For a sequel, upgrade every element substantially, not just a few.
why: Melee's concept was simply to power up Smash by leaps and bounds, and upgrading fighters, stages, graphics, sound, play feel and more made it eye-opening.
how: List all of the game's elements and set a clear upgrade goal for each, using the new hardware's headroom.
example: Super Smash Bros. Melee on GameCube.
quote: That was, of course, to power up Smash Bros. by leaps and bounds!

title: Meteos
principle: Make each stage or character change the rules, not just the visuals
why: In most puzzle games character choice barely changes play, while Meteos planets differ in block shapes, field width, launch behavior and audio, so controls feel different and players pick favorites.
how: Give each stage or character distinct parameters such as field size, gravity, speed and piece types, plus its own music and sound effects.
anti_pattern: Character select that only swaps art or slightly alters skills.
example: Meteos planets: Boggob gains height each jump, Hevendor blocks vanish on match, Brabbit moves very slowly.
quote: The controls feel drastically different when you switch planets, so I'm sure players had their favorites.

title: Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking
principle: Sell a creature fantasy with small, believable behaviors
why: Depicting the Mushi grazing on its meal instead of scarfing it instantly gave a stronger sense of raising a pet, and hidden behaviors add depth.
how: Animate everyday actions over time and add hidden responses, like a pet adjusting its schedule to when it is woken.
example: Sodatete! Kouchuu Ouja Mushiking: grazing on food; waking it early shifts its schedule.
quote: For example, instead of having it instantly scarf down food, we depicted it grazing on its meal to capture that "pet" feeling.

title: Kid Icarus: Uprising
principle: Aim your concept at the hardware's strengths and the market gap
why: Touch! Generations already covered casual DS players, so Sakurai made a meaty game for hardcore players, and glasses-free 3D made depth central, leading to a TPS reimagined like Smash reimagined fighting games.
how: List what the platform uniquely does and which audiences are already served, then target the gap and rethink the genre's by-the-book conventions.
anti_pattern: Making a genre game that follows by-the-book theory.

title: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate
principle: Pick the bold concept your production continuity makes uniquely affordable
why: Earlier Smash games rebuilt everything with new teams, but Ultimate kept Bandai Namco's team and dev environment on similar hardware, so bringing back every fighter became feasible; Sakurai saw it as the one chance to do it.
how: Before choosing a sequel's headline concept, take stock of what carries over (team, tools, assets, hardware architecture) and aim at what that makes possible.
example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate — 'Everyone is here!'
quote: I knew if there would ever be a chance to include everyone, this would be it!

title: Faithfulness Comes First in Licensed Games
principle: Invent freely where the source shows little
why: Licensed characters can't be changed much, but those with little shown action leave room to design.
how: Identify characters or elements the source barely defines and create their moves there.
example: In Super Smash Bros., pilots Fox and Captain Falcon gave freedom, producing the Falcon Punch.
